issues.legal_issue: For a specific-performance suit, a contractual period stated as a relative interval rather than a definite calendar date does not make that interval a date fixed for performance under the first part of the limitation rule.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance of an agreement to sell.
The agreement required payment of the balance within six months of its execution and provided for execution of the sale deed upon payment; it did not specify a calendar date for performance.
The High Court treated the expiry of the six-month period as the date fixed for performance and held the suit time-barred under the first part of the limitation rule.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in applying the first part of the limitation rule. Since the agreement did not fix a definite calendar date for performance, the limitation period runs from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused, and the suit was not barred on the basis adopted by the High Court.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 54 of Schedule I to the Limitation Act, 1963, where a definite date is fixed for performance, limitation runs from that date; where no such date is fixed, it runs from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. In Ahmadsahab Abdul Mulla (2) (Dead) v. Bibijan, (2009) 5 SCC 462, the Court held that a date fixed for performance is a crystallized, specified calendar date. Rathnavathi v. Kavita Ganashamdas, (2015) 5 SCC 223, applied the distinction between a date fixed and a contract without such a date.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.agreement_specifies_relative_period_only: The agreement stated a period measured from an event, rather than specifying a definite calendar date for performance.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks specific performance and the agreement states only a relative period for performance, limitation runs from the claimant's notice that performance is refused.

issues.legal_issue: A court hearing a first appeal from a trial judgment must decide all issues and consider the evidence, rather than dispose of the appeal solely on a preliminary issue of limitation.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the suit on its merits while deciding the limitation issue in the claimant's favour.
The claimant filed a first appeal from the trial judgment.
The High Court addressed only limitation, held the suit time-barred, and did not decide the remaining issues or the merits of the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was required to consider all issues in the first appeal. Because it considered only limitation, its judgment was set aside and the matter was remanded for decision of the remaining issues on their merits.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a court sitting as a court of first appeal has a duty to deal with all issues and the evidence before recording its findings. The Court relied on Vinod Kumar v. Gangadhar, (2015) 1 SCC 391, which relied particularly on Madhukar v. Sangram, (2001) 4 SCC 756.

predicates.first_appeal_from_trial_judgment: A party brought a first appeal from a trial court's judgment.
predicates.appellate_court_decided_only_limitation: The first appellate court decided the appeal solely on limitation without addressing the remaining issues and evidence.

issues.definition: When a first appeal from a trial judgment is decided solely on limitation, the first appellate court must decide all issues and consider the evidence.
